skill: Solve a Bernoulli ODE by reduction to a first-order linear ODE and integrating factors; select its general solution.
reasoning_steps: Normalize the ODE to y' + p(x)y = q(x)y^n.
Identify n, multiply by y^(-n), and set z=y^(1-n); the chain rule gives z' +(1-n)p z=(1-n)q.
Compute an elementary integrating factor, integrate the product derivative, and introduce an arbitrary constant.
Substitute back, invert the power with appropriate real branches/domains, and distinguish the resulting solution from distractors.
response_contract: Observed practice questions have one five-choice math radio field keyed selection. Canonical example has worked solution but no answer field. Do not infer free-entry requirements.
difficulty: Six moderate cases begin in standard form; five hard cases require normalization, with rational powers. Elementary exponentials/powers and one integration-by-parts case are evidenced.
invariants: Bernoulli reduction, linear integrating factor, elementary integration, and return to y.
Single general-solution target, one correct radio choice, five math choices for observed practice.
n is nontrivial (not 0 or 1); solution valid on intervals where divisions and real powers make sense.
Comparable algebraic workload; no initial conditions or new transcendental integrals.
permitted_variations: Eligible answer-bearing coefficients and signs in p and q may vary jointly with integrating factor, particular solution, and distractors.
Power n may vary among demonstrated nontrivial powers with comparable inversions; no fixed correct root degree or denominator sign is essential.
For power-law/exponential families vary coefficients and simple exponents while keeping integration elementary.
Shuffle answer positions and vary which near-miss formula is correct as mathematical evidence changes; source correct positions are incidental.
Equivalent scaled arbitrary constants are permitted; they must not create multiple equivalent choices.

lesson_passages: The substitution $z=y^{1-n}$ reduces any Bernoulli equation to a first-order linear differential equation.
This differential equation is linear, so we can use integrating factors to solve it.

source_cases.problem:
Find the general solution to the differential equation

$$
\dfrac {\textrm{d}y} {\textrm{d}x} + \dfrac{y}{x}  = \dfrac{x^2}{y} .
$$

Find the general solution to the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-y={y}^{2}{e}^{x}.
$$

Find the general solution to the differential equation
$x^{2}\frac{dy}{dx} = y^{4} - xy$.

Find the general solution to the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+xy=x{y}^{2}.
$$

Find the general solution to the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-3{x}^{2}y={x}^{2}{y}^{-4}.
$$

Find the general solution to the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y=-x{y}^{3}.
$$

Find the general solution to the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-y=\sqrt{y}.
$$

Find the general solution to the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-\frac{y}{x}=\sqrt{x}\,{y}^{2}.
$$

Find the general solution to the differential equation

$$
x\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y={x}^{2}{y}^{3/4}.
$$

Find the general solution to the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{2}+2xy}{{x}^{2}}.
$$

Find the general solution to the differential equation

$$
{x}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{y}}-xy.
$$

Find the general solution to the differential equation

$$
{x}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={x}^{3}{y}^{2}+xy.
$$
